title: Educational Leadership
summary: Learn to lead schools and departments: leadership roles, vision and improvement planning, leading teaching and learning, managing people and budgets, using data for decisions, and community partnerships and ethical leadership.
audience: Principals, deputies, heads of department, aspiring school leaders and education students

body.p: School leaders, including principals, deputies, heads of department and senior teachers, shape the conditions in which teachers teach and learners learn. Research consistently finds that leadership is one of the most important school-level influences on learning, mainly through its effect on teaching quality.

list: Setting direction: a shared vision, clear priorities and high expectations.
Instructional leadership: improving teaching and learning through curriculum oversight, classroom support and professional development.
Developing people: supporting, motivating and growing staff.
Managing the organisation: timetables, finances, facilities, safety and records.
Building relationships with learners, families, communities and education authorities.

body.p: Leadership is not only the principal's job. Distributed leadership shares responsibility with heads of department, teacher leaders, learner leaders and governing bodies, which builds capacity and sustainability.

body.tip: Spend some time in classrooms every week; leaders who know what teaching looks like make better decisions.

body.p: A school improvement plan turns a vision into priorities, actions and measurable targets. Effective plans focus on a few priorities rather than many.

steps: Analyse the current situation using data: results, attendance, learner and parent views, inspection reports.
Choose two or three priorities with the biggest impact on learning.
Plan actions, responsibilities, timelines and resources.

body.p: If 62% of learners passed mathematics last year and the target is 70%, that is an increase of 8 percentage points, a relative improvement of about 8 / 62, or 12.9%. Be clear which kind of increase you mean. Targets should be ambitious but realistic and backed by specific actions, such as extra support for learners just below the pass mark and joint lesson planning.

body.tip: Display the school's priorities where staff, learners and parents can see them, and report progress each term.

body.p: Improving teaching is the most direct way leaders improve learning.

list: Classroom observation and feedback focused on development, not judgement alone; agree one or two specific improvements at a time.
Professional learning communities: teachers meet regularly to plan, share practice and examine learners' work.
Coaching and mentoring, especially for new teachers.
Protecting teaching time: start lessons on time, reduce interruptions and limit administrative loads.
Monitoring curriculum coverage and assessment quality.

body.p: Schools improve where staff trust each other, talk openly about teaching, try new strategies and learn from evidence. Leaders build this by modelling learning themselves, recognising effort and treating mistakes as part of improvement.

body.tip: Ask "What are learners learning, and how do we know?" in every meeting about teaching.

body.p: Leaders manage staff, money, time and facilities, often with limited resources.

list: Recruit carefully and induct new staff well.
Set clear expectations and give regular, fair feedback.
Support staff wellbeing and manage workload.
Address poor performance early, with support and clear procedures.
Follow employment law and agreements with unions.

body.p: Use simple indicators to plan. A school of 800 learners with an annual non-staff budget of R1 200 000 has R1500 per learner. With 25 teachers, the learner-teacher ratio is 800 / 25 = 32. Budget around priorities, involve the governing body, keep transparent records and follow procurement rules.

list: Timetables should reflect curriculum time requirements and priorities.
Maintain buildings, water and sanitation for safety and dignity.
Track textbooks and equipment to reduce loss.

body.tip: Publish a simple summary of the school budget to staff and parents; transparency builds trust and support.

body.p: Data helps leaders see problems early and target support, but numbers need interpretation and context.

list: Attendance: with 800 learners and 92% average daily attendance, about 736 attend and 64 are absent each day; patterns by grade, day or individual show where to act.
Assessment results by class, subject, gender and other groups reveal gaps.
Learner progress over time matters more than single results.
Surveys of learners, staff and parents capture experiences numbers miss.
Discipline and safety incidents show where support is needed.

body.p: Use data to ask questions, not to blame. If one class's results fall, find out why: absent teachers, a difficult topic, timetable problems or learners' circumstances. Protect learners' privacy when sharing data.

body.tip: Choose a small set of indicators and review them at every leadership meeting.

body.p: Schools serve communities. Strong partnerships with families and local organisations support learners' attendance, behaviour and achievement.

list: Communicate regularly and in languages families understand.
Invite parents to learn about the curriculum and how to support learning at home.
Work with health services, social workers, businesses and community leaders.
Support the school governing body or board to fulfil its role in policy, finances and accountability.
Put learners' interests first in every decision.
Be fair and transparent in appointments, promotions and admissions.
Manage public funds honestly and reject corruption.
Protect learners: safeguarding policies, anti-bullying measures and swift action on abuse.
Promote inclusion so every learner can belong and succeed.

body.p: Leading change, such as a new curriculum or digital tools, requires explaining the purpose, involving staff, providing training and resources, and celebrating early successes.

body.tip: Ask, "How would this decision look to a learner, a parent and a teacher?" before finalising it.

quiz.q: Leadership mainly improves learning through its effect on:
Sharing leadership with heads of department and teacher leaders is called:
A good improvement plan focuses on:
Raising a pass rate from 62% to 70% is an increase of:
As a relative improvement, that is about:

options: Teachers meeting regularly to improve practice together
